Copies columns of the map from the ring buffer at $8000-$84FF (25 rows of $30 bytes, X the ring column to start at) into the screen not being shown ($7400 when $17 is 0, $7000 otherwise), from screen column Y up to the end column patched into $E0F1/$E197, one row at a time unrolled. Spreading the copy over the eight frames of a scroll step keeps each frame's share small.
The end column of the copy into screen $7000, the operand of CPY # at $E0F0, patched by each phase (from $E1CD, or $EE7F while stopped); the copy into $7400 follows.
The end column of the copy into screen $7400, the operand of CPY # at $E196.

One frame's share of the scroll, by the fine-scroll phase $18: at phase 7 builds the next map column into the ring buffer ($E1D4); at 6 also moves the star characters on ($E316); then copies this phase's columns of the hidden screen (from $E1CC: 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 to 40) from the ring position $1B onward, so the hidden screen is complete, one column further on, when the screens swap.
The screen column at which each fine-scroll phase's copy starts, and (the next entry) where it ends: 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 40.
The phase-start table read one on, as each phase's end column.

Builds the next 25-character column of the map into the ring buffer, at ring column $1B + 40: the map is five rows of tiles, each tile 5 by 5 characters. $21 is the tile column and $20 the character column inside the tile (0-4, $21 moving on after 4). For each of the five tile rows the tile number comes from that row's table ($3934, $3A34, $3B34, $3C34, $3D34, indexed by $21, patched into $E21F/$E220 from $E2CC/$E2D1), its address from $3E34/$3EFC, and the five characters of the column from it (row steps from $E2B8). A space ($20) is replaced by the star character of that screen row from $E2FD, so the starfield shows through the gaps.
Low byte of the tile-row table read at $E21E (LDY $3934,X), $34 for each row.
High byte of the tile-row table, stepped from $39 to $3D for the five tile rows (from $E2D1).
Low byte of where the tile's first character row goes in the ring buffer: the new column, $1B + 40 wrapped at 42.
High byte of the first character row's place: $80 for the top tile row, one more for each tile row down.
Low byte of the second character row's place, the column plus $30.
High byte of the second character row's place.
Low byte of the third character row's place, the column plus $60.
High byte of the third character row's place.
Low byte of the fourth character row's place, the column plus $90.
High byte of the fourth character row's place.
Low byte of the fifth character row's place, the column plus $C0.
High byte of the fifth character row's place; then the next tile row is set up.
Offsets of the next row inside a 5-by-5 tile (the index plus 5), then at $E2CC/$E2D1 the low and high bytes of the five tile-row tables ($3934-$3D34).
Low bytes of the five tile-row tables, all $34.
High bytes of the five tile-row tables, $39 to $3D.
Fills characters 0-$20 of the play character set ($7800-$7907) with $FF, the blank background the star characters draw into.

The starfield, one entry per screen row: at $E2E4 its kind (0 none, 1 far, 2 near) and at $E2FD the character it shows now (a space, $20, where the row has no star). Then at $E338 the last and at $E33B the first character of each kind's cycle (1-$0F far, $10-$1F near).
The star character each screen row shows now (a space, $20, where it has none), stepped by star_chars_step.
Moves each row's star character on to the next of its cycle ($01-$0F or $10-$1F), wrapping to the first: each character holds the star a little further along, so the stars slide behind the scenery.

Steps the fine scroll $18 down by one pixel. At zero ($E345) it goes back to 7, moves the ring position $1B on (wrapping after $29) and swaps the screens: $17 flips and $24, the video chip's screen and character setting, goes to $CE (screen $7000) or $DE (screen $7400).

Used instead of the scroll while it is stopped ($52): copies five columns a frame (from $EE7E) of the ring buffer into the hidden screen at the same ring position, and swaps the screens every eight frames, so the playfield stays redrawn without moving.

Gives each newly placed object ($FF1C set) its properties from the level's object-type tables, by its type in $FDB4: colour ($FD14) and group (the high nibble, $FFD0) from $03E6, first frame ($FD28, $FE90) from $0200, last frame ($FEA4) from $02A2, firing mode ($FF94), frame delay (bits 2-5, $FECC/$FEB8) and ping-pong flag (bit 6, $FEF4) from $0344, and hit points ($FEE0) from $0488. All four shot objects (16-19) are done in one call, at most one enemy.

Starts the attack waves placed at this point of the level: when the scroll's tile column $21 changes and $142C has a wave there, the wave number ($152C), its size less one ($162C) and its list (address from $182C/$172C) give each enemy five bytes: x, y, type, path and delay. Each goes into a free object (0-15, no state and no delay) just off the right edge (x high bit set) and is marked new. An entry of type 6 is given no delay when the second ship is the drone, and an object with no delay never comes to life, so those pods only appear in a two-player game.

Keeps the objects to the visible area: an object inside it (x $008-$14F) that was waiting (state 1) takes its real state from $FDB4; outside it, an enemy or pod (state 5 or more) waits in state 1, unseen and untouchable, unless it has gone off the left edge ($1F0-$1F8), where it is removed; a shot or burst (states 2-4) outside is removed.

Puts each ship in play on its hardware sprite (player 1 on sprite 0, the second ship on 1): x and the x high bit ($02/$0A, $03/$0B), y ($04, $05), frame into both screens' pointers ($06, $07) and colour ($08, $09).

In a two-player game (both in play, the second not the drone) records in $2D where ship 1 stands against ship 2 on the grid of character cells: bit 4 the same row, bit 0 one row below, bit 1 one row above; bit 5 the same column, bit 2 one or two columns to the right, bit 3 one or two to the left. The movement uses it to make the ships push each other.

Moves the ships from cell to cell of an 8-pixel grid: rows $2E/$2F (1-23) and columns $30/$31 (2-36). The sticks are read inverted into $32/$33; when a ship is not already gliding in a direction and the stick asks for it, its row or column changes by one and a glide of 8 pixels starts (a counter of $34-$3B, frames from $E9B4 by the ship's step). With two players, a ship moving into the other (by $2D) pushes it a cell the same way unless the other is pushing back or already moving; a ship against the other at the edge does not move. The drone ($B00E = 4) is moved elsewhere ($9E78).

Glides the ships toward their new cells: each running counter of $34-$3B (up, down, left, right for ship 1, then the same for ship 2) moves its ship by the ship's step ($3C vertical and $40 horizontal for ship 1, $3D and $41 for ship 2), carrying into the x high bit; when a pair has run out the step goes back to the ship's own speed ($3E/$42, $3F/$43, always 2).
Frames a glide of one cell (8 pixels) takes, indexed by the step: step 1 takes 8, 2 takes 4, 4 takes 2 and 8 takes 1.

While ship 1 is hit (state 1): every fourth frame shows the next frame of its explosion from $EA18 ($5A from 12 down: frames $2E-$37 then nothing), with sounds 0, 1 and 2 at the start; at the end takes a life with DEC $B005 at $E9F3, the instruction the check at $F77D guards. With a life left the ship comes back invulnerable (state 3, frame 3); with none it is out (state 0), and when the second ship is out too, or is the drone, the game ends through the vector at $66 ($A000, back to the front end).
Takes one of ship 1's lives: DEC $B005 (CE 05 B0), the three bytes the anti-cheat check compares.
The DEC's low address byte, $05, as the anti-cheat check reads it.
The DEC's high address byte, $B0, as the anti-cheat check reads it.
BMI after the DEC (its opcode $30 is checked too): below 0 lives ship 1 is out of play; otherwise it comes back invulnerable.
The sprite frames of an exploding ship, read from the end: $2E up to $37, then $BF (an empty frame) three times.
The same as ship1_hit_sequence for the second ship ($5B, $5D, lives taken with DEC $B006 at $EA57, back with frame $0A); the game ends when ship 1 is already out.
Takes one of ship 2's lives: DEC $B006 (CE 06 B0), checked by the anti-cheat check.
The second DEC's low address byte, $06.
The second DEC's high address byte, $B0.
BMI after ship 2's DEC, also checked: below 0 lives ship 2 is out, and the game ends if ship 1 is too.

While ship 1 is invulnerable (state 3): counts $56 down and flashes the ship through the six colours at $EAA3, one a frame; at zero it is back in normal play (state 2, colour $0E) and $56 is preset to $C0, so the next return after a hit is invulnerable for 192 frames (about 3.8 seconds). An unchanged pod sets $56 to $FF instead, 255 frames, about 5.1 seconds; the level start leaves 102 there ($A260).
The colours an invulnerable ship flashes through: six for ship 1, then at $EAAA six for ship 2.
Ship 2's six flash colours.
The same as ship1_invulnerable for the second ship ($57, $59, colours from $EAAA, colour $0A in normal play).
Runs each ship's hit or invulnerability sequence by its state ($B00D, $B00E): 1 the explosion, 3 the flashing; the drone (4) has neither.

The generators, once a frame: for player 1 a counter ($64) runs from 0 up to the table's value for the number of generators ($EB73 by $B018: 60, 50, 40, 30 or 18) and then ticks, so a tick comes every 61, 51, 41, 31 or 19 frames. Each tick moves the rebuild count $60 up by one, to 7. Once it is at 7, each further tick fills one battery that is not full to its six charges (7) and starts the rebuild again; when no battery is left to fill (an empty slot is skipped), the generator's own charge $62 is set to 6. The same for player 2 ($65, $61, $63, $B014-$B017). Firing a super weapon from the generator's charge restarts the rebuild.

The generator counter's limit by the number of generators 0-4: 60, 50, 40, 30, 18. The counter runs from 0 to this value, so a tick comes every 61, 51, 41, 31 or 19 frames; seven ticks rebuild the generator and an eighth fills a battery.

Moves the players' shots one place on the frames between whole-character scrolls. The shots are characters drawn into the screen being shown: 20 slots at $FDF0 (0-9 player 1, 10-19 player 2, or the drone), each with its column $FE04, row $FE18, the character under it $FE2C, its own character $FE40, its step $FE54 (+1 or -1), vertical if $FE68 is set, and a just-fired flag $FE7C. Each puts back the character it covered, moves, and ends at the edge of the screen or on a solid character ($21-$F5); on another shot's character it is not drawn; otherwise it draws itself.
Low bytes of the row-address tables of the screen being shown, by $17: $A0 ($85A0, screen $7000) or $B9 ($85B9, screen $7400).

Moves the players' shots each frame: points $27/$28 at the row table of the screen being shown, then, except on the frame the screen moves a whole character ($18 = 7), steps them ($EB78). On that frame the shot also moves one column left with the scenery (unless the scroll is stopped, $52), nothing is put back (the screen was just redrawn), and a shot moving right clears the copy of itself one column behind.

Player 1's fire button ($78 bit 4, 0 when pressed), when the ship is in play. Pressing fires the normal weapons ($F1C3), and so does letting go. Held for 15 frames, it tries the super weapon chosen in $49: it needs enough free shot slots (10, 5 or 2, from $EE73) and its cost in charges ($F486: 2, 2, 1), taken from the generator's charge $62 when that is enough (which restarts the rebuild) or else from a battery holding more than the cost; then the weapon's sounds and its shots ($ED9D), and held on it fires again 7 frames later ($45 = 8). Without the slots or the charges it keeps trying ($45 = 15).
Not a routine of the game: $ED09 is the KERNAL's TALK, which the fast loader calls with the ROM in. In RAM it falls inside ship1_fire's JSR $F1C3.
$ED0C is the KERNAL's LISTEN; in RAM it is the operand of ship1_fire's LDA #$00, and the end of ship1_fire follows.
The same as ship1_fire for player 2 ($79, $46, $4A, $63, $B014-$B017, $71), when the second ship is a player and in play.

Starts player 1's super-weapon shots: the pattern of weapon $49 (address from $EE76/$EE7A) gives four bytes a shot, its step, column and row offsets from the ship and its character, until $80; each goes into a free slot from 9 down, skipping any that would start off the screen. With the drone in play, the drone then fires its own line ($EE13 with pattern 3).
$EDB9 is the KERNAL's SECOND; in RAM it is the operand of a CMP #$04 in ship1_super_shots.
$EDC7 is the KERNAL's TKSA; in RAM it is the BEQ of ship1_super_shots that ends the pattern at $80.
$EDDD is the KERNAL's CIOUT; in RAM it is ship1_super_shots' loop over the free slots, which goes on to place each shot.
Starts player 2's super-weapon shots (pattern Y from $EE76/$EE7A, offsets from $31/$2F, slots 10-19). With Y = 3 it is the drone's line of five shots when player 1 fires a super weapon.

Free shot slots each super weapon needs, less one: 9, 4, 1. At $EE76 and $EE7A the low and high bytes of the shot patterns ($F07D, $F0AF, $F0A6, and the drone's $F471); at $EE7E the column each frame of a stopped scroll's redraw starts at (0, 5, 10 ... 40).
Low bytes of the shot patterns: $7D, $AF, $A6, and $71 for the drone.
High bytes of the shot patterns: $F0, $F0, $F0, $F4.
The first column of each stopped-scroll phase's copy (0).
The column table read one on: each stopped-scroll phase's end column (5, 10 ... 40).
Part of enemies_follow_paths: while an enemy's step timer runs, it counts down by one and the enemy keeps its speeds.

Moves the 16 enemy objects along their paths, on the frames when $68 is 0, so every second frame: when an enemy's step timer $FDDC runs out, the next step of its path ($FDC8 picks one of 80, at $C4 the place in it) gives three bytes: the x speed (bits 0-2, bit 7 the direction) with flags for half speed ($FF58, bit 3), firing ($FF80, bit 4) and animation ($FF6C, bit 5); the y speed (bits 0-2 and 7) with half speed ($FD64, bit 3); and how many calls the step lasts, less one, so a third byte of b holds the step for 2 x (b + 1) frames. The speeds themselves are applied every frame (objects_move). Paths 0-$41 have 16 steps and repeat; paths from $42 run on for 32 steps, into the next path's bytes. Exploding enemies (state 2) keep following their paths.
The sounds each super weapon plays when fired: voice 2 effects 4, 6, 8 ($EF31) and voice 3 effects 5, 7, 9 ($EF34).
The voice 3 sounds of the super weapons: 5, 7, 9.
Builds the path addresses: 80 paths of 48 bytes from $052C, low bytes at $8500 and high bytes at $8550 (the working bytes at $EF65/$EF66).
The working address of paths_table_build: high byte, then low byte.
Low byte of the path address being built.

Builds the tables that turn an object's y into a screen row for the collision tests: high bytes for screen $7000 at $8600 and for $7400 at $8700, low bytes at $9500. The first 50 entries give row 0, then each row takes 8, and from entry 234 on row 23 is repeated.
Builds $9600, which turns an object's x (halved) into a screen column: entries 0-11 hold their own index, then each column from 1 takes four entries, up to $AB; the rest are 0.

Part of objects_animate for an exploding object (state 2): steps its frame through the burst, $2E to $37, and removes it after $37. An enemy (objects 0-15) steps on every second call, by $FEB8, so every fourth frame; an enemy shot (16-19) on every call, every second frame. A frame outside $2E-$37 becomes $2E.
Two bytes no path reaches: a BCS $EFFB (B0 EA) left after the JMP before it.
Part of object_burst_step: the burst's last frame has gone, so the object is removed (state 0, firing off).

Animates every object in play, on the frames when $68 is 1, so every second frame: a burst steps on ($EFE8); an object with its animation flag ($FF6C) changes frame on every ($FECC + 1)th call, every 2 x ($FECC + 1) frames, from its first frame ($FE90) to its last ($FEA4) and back to the first, or with its ping-pong flag ($FEF4) back down again. Then runs the anti-cheat check ($F77D).

The super weapons' shots, four bytes each (step, column offset, row offset, character), each list ending with $80. Weapon 0 ($F07D): ten shots of character $FE in the ship's row, three columns apart, a line across the screen that also starts beyond any wall. Weapon 2 ($F0A6): two shots of character $FF side by side. Weapon 1 ($F0AF): five shots of characters $FD and $FC, two ahead above and below, one backward, and two from behind two rows above and below.

With the drone in play, fires its copies of player 1's normal weapons into slots 10-19: forward shots (up to $4B + 1, character $F6) and trident ($47, character $FA, rows above and below) from the drone's place ($31, $2F), tail fire ($4D, character $F9) from the drone's row, and the vertical cannon ($4F, characters $F7/$F8), which starts one column behind player 1's ship, not from the drone.

Fires player 1's normal weapons, each only when its slots are free: a forward shot (character $F6) into the first free of slots 0 to $4B, so $4B + 1 can be in flight (two at the start of a level, four at most, six with converge, which takes the tail's slots 4-5), with sounds $10 and $11; the vertical cannon ($4F): a pair up and down (characters $F7/$F8, slots 8-9); the trident ($47): a pair one column behind, a row above and below, firing forward (character $FA, slots 6-7); tail fire ($4D): a pair a row above and below, firing backward (character $F9, slots 4-5). The same as ship1_normal_fire for player 2: slots 10-19, forward up to $4C + 1, vertical $50, trident $48, tail $4E, from $31/$2F.

Sorts the 20 objects by y for the multiplexer, using the stack page as a bucket table. The page is all $FF; for each object, from 19 down, the stack pointer is set to its y halved, PLA skips forward to the first $FF, and PHA puts the object's number there. Then the page from $0119 is read upward: each number found goes into the sorted list $EC-$FF and its byte is put back to $FF. So the page is left as it was, which is what the stack check at $AFAE relies on: any other byte in $0138-$013F means something else has used the stack.

Moves each object in play by its speeds: y by $FD78 and x by $FD8C (bits 0-6 the speed, bit 7 the direction), the x carrying into its high bit $FD3C; with the half-speed flags ($FD64, $FF58) a direction only moves on alternate frames ($68).

Draws the far stars, one character of 1-15 a scroll step: a pixel cleared from the $FF background at the fine-scroll phase's place ($F6ED), moving on a double pixel every two frames; at phase 6 the next character takes it ($C2 counts through $F6DD).
Offsets of characters 0-15 in the character set (n x 8), for the star routines; then at $F6ED the far star's byte by fine-scroll phase.
The far star's byte at each fine-scroll phase: FE FE FB FB EF EF BF BF, a double pixel cleared from the $FF background.

Draws the near stars in characters $10-$1F: a single cleared pixel ($F727) that moves one pixel a call and passes to the next character every eight calls ($C0, $C3). stars_animate calls it only on the frames when $68 is 1, so the star moves a pixel every second frame and changes character every 16 frames.
The near star's byte for each of its eight steps: one pixel cleared, moving left.

Runs the starfield chosen on the title with F3 ($B02F): setting 2 alternates the near and far stars frame by frame, setting 1 draws only the far stars every other frame, setting 0 alternates the near stars with the far stars running the other way.

Protection, run every second frame at the end of objects_animate: checks that the two instructions that take a life are untouched, DEC $B005 at $E9F3 (CE 05 B0) and DEC $B006 at $EA57 (CE 06 B0), and that the BMI after each still reads $30. If anything differs, as after the infinite-lives poke POKE 59891,173 (which turns the first DEC into LDA), it switches the KERNAL ROM in over the game ($01 = $37). Its own JMP back is then never fetched: the next instruction comes from the ROM at $F7B6, and the machine runs off into a loop through zero page with interrupts off, so the game freezes (measured).

One voice's effect: a request starts at once if it is 0-3, if it is 4-15 and what plays is 4 or higher or has ended, or if it is 16-31 and what plays is 16 or higher or has ended, so lower numbers win. Starting sets every register and setting from the effect's tables. Otherwise the playing effect steps on ($FAF1).
Steps a playing effect: counts its gate frames down and then switches to its after-gate waveform (the gate off), counts the release down, then runs its pulse sweep, frequency sweep and special kind.

The processor's NMI, reset and IRQ vectors, used because the game runs with the KERNAL ROM banked out: in the front end NMI $B1BF (an RTI, so RESTORE does nothing) and IRQ $B128 (title_irq); in play NMI $A07B (irq_exit's RTI, set at $A1E8) and IRQ $A05F; during a load IRQ $B702 (loading_irq_setup). No instruction writes the reset vector.
